summary: Defines Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE), which protects CoAP at the application layer using COSE. It gives end-to-end protection between endpoints, even through proxies, and suits constrained devices. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: OSCORE lets two small devices talk to each other so that nobody in the middle, including any proxy that forwards the messages, can read or change what they say. It hides the interesting parts of each message, encrypts them, and leaves only what a forwarder needs in the open.

questions: object security for constrained restful environments
how does oscore differ from dtls
how does oscore prevent replay attacks
subtitle: Application-layer encryption for CoAP that stays intact end to end, even when proxies sit in the middle.

tldr.problem: CoAP is normally secured with DTLS or TLS, which end at every proxy, so a proxy can read, change, drop or reorder the messages it forwards.
tldr.mechanism: OSCORE wraps the sensitive parts of a CoAP request or response in a compressed COSE object protected with an AEAD algorithm, and leaves only the fields a proxy needs in the clear.
tldr.outcome: Client and server get end-to-end encryption, integrity, replay protection and binding of each response to its request, with a small per-message overhead. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7252.

today: RFC 8613 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2019. It updates RFC 7252, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC says OSCORE may be used over UDP or TCP, with non-IP transports, and alongside TLS or DTLS on one or more hops of the path.

sections.title: Why Another Security Protocol for CoAP
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol is a web transfer protocol designed for constrained nodes and networks, and CoAP may be mapped from HTTP. CoAP specifies the use of proxies for scalability and efficiency and references DTLS for security. CoAP-to-CoAP, HTTP-to-CoAP and CoAP-to-HTTP proxies require DTLS or TLS to be terminated at the proxy. The proxy therefore not only has access to the data required for performing the intended proxy functionality, but is also able to eavesdrop on, or manipulate, any part of the message payload and metadata in transit between the endpoints. The proxy can also inject, delete or reorder packets, since they are no longer protected by DTLS or TLS.

OSCORE, the Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments, protects CoAP and CoAP-mappable HTTP requests and responses end to end across intermediary nodes such as CoAP forward proxies and cross-protocol translators. In addition to the core CoAP features, OSCORE supports the Observe, Block-wise and No-Response options, as well as the PATCH and FETCH methods. OSCORE essentially protects the RESTful interactions: the request method, the requested resource, the message payload and so on. It protects neither the CoAP messaging layer nor the CoAP Token, which may change between the endpoints.

OSCORE works in very constrained nodes and networks, thanks to its small message size and the restricted code and memory requirements in addition to what CoAP already needs. It may be used over any underlying layer, such as UDP or TCP, and with non-IP transports, and may also be used in different ways with HTTP.

The technical solution builds on CBOR Object Signing and Encryption, providing end-to-end encryption, integrity, replay protection and binding of response to request, with a compressed version of COSE used to keep the overhead small. The use of OSCORE is signaled in CoAP with a new option and in HTTP with a new header field and content type. An implementation supporting this specification MAY implement only the client part, only the server part, or only one of the proxy parts.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary web security stops at every proxy, because the proxy has to decrypt the traffic to forward it. OSCORE is designed so that the proxy can forward the traffic without ever being able to read it.

sections.title: The OSCORE Option
sections.content:
The OSCORE option indicates that the CoAP message is an OSCORE message and that it contains a compressed COSE object. It has option number 9 in the CoAP option space, is critical, safe to forward, part of the cache key, and not repeatable.

The option value carries the OSCORE flag bits, the Sender Sequence Number, the Sender ID, and the ID Context when these fields are present. If the flag bits are all zero, the option value SHALL be empty, with an option length of 0. An endpoint receiving a CoAP message without payload that also contains an OSCORE option SHALL treat it as malformed and reject it. A successful response to a request with the OSCORE option SHALL contain the OSCORE option; whether error responses contain it depends on the error type.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender marks the message with a short option saying that the body is protected. Proxies can see the option and forward the message without understanding what is inside.

sections.title: The Security Context
sections.content:
OSCORE requires that client and server establish a shared security context, which is the set of information elements needed to carry out the cryptographic operations. For each endpoint the context is composed of a Common Context, a Sender Context and a Recipient Context. The endpoints protect messages to send using the Sender Context and verify messages received using the Recipient Context.

An endpoint uses its Sender ID to derive its Sender Context, and the other endpoint uses the same ID, now called the Recipient ID, to derive its Recipient Context. The two contexts identified by the same IDs in the two endpoints are not the same, but they are partly mirrored, and both endpoints need to be able to retrieve the right context to use.

The Common Context holds the AEAD algorithm, the HKDF algorithm used to derive the keys, the Master Secret, the optional Master Salt, the optional ID Context, and the Common IV used to generate the AEAD nonce. The Sender Context holds the Sender ID, the Sender Key used to protect outgoing messages, and the Sender Sequence Number, which enumerates requests and certain responses and is used as the Partial IV to generate unique nonces. The Recipient Context holds the Recipient ID, the Recipient Key used to verify incoming messages, and, on the server, the Replay Window.

All parameters except the Sender Sequence Number and the Replay Window are immutable once the context is established. An endpoint may free up memory by not storing the Common IV, Sender Key and Recipient Key and deriving them when needed, or by not storing the Master Secret and Master Salt after the other parameters have been derived. Endpoints MAY operate as both client and server with the same context, and the endpoints MUST NOT change the Sender or Recipient ID when changing roles.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends share one secret and derive from it everything they need: a key for sending, a key for receiving, and a starting value for the nonce. The two ends hold the mirror image of each other's keys.

sections.title: Deriving the Keys
sections.content:
Each endpoint derives the parameters of the security context from a small set of input parameters. The Master Secret, the Sender ID and the Recipient ID SHALL be preestablished. The AEAD Algorithm, the Master Salt, the HKDF Algorithm and the Replay Window MAY be preestablished, and where they are not, a default is used: the AEAD algorithm defaults to AES-CCM-16-64-128, with the COSE algorithm encoding 10; the Master Salt defaults to the empty byte string; the HKDF algorithm defaults to HKDF SHA-256; and the default replay mechanism is an anti-replay sliding window with a window size of 32. All input parameters need to be known and agreed on by both endpoints, but the Replay Window may differ between them.

The Sender Key, Recipient Key and Common IV SHALL be derived with the HMAC-based HKDF, which consists of the HKDF-Extract and HKDF-Expand steps: the output parameter is HKDF with the Master Salt as salt, the Master Secret as input keying material, and an info value that is a CBOR array holding the ID, the ID Context or nil, the AEAD algorithm, a type label of "Key" or "IV", and the size of the key or nonce in bytes. HKDF SHA-256 is mandatory to implement.

For the default algorithms the extract phase produces a pseudorandom key as HMAC-SHA-256 of the Master Salt and the Master Secret. With AES-CCM-16-64-128, the algorithm value is 10, the length L is 16 for keys and 13 for the Common IV, and because L is smaller than the hash output the expand phase is a single HMAC invocation, so the Sender Key, Recipient Key and Common IV are the first 16 or 13 bytes of the output.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared secret is stretched into the actual encryption keys using a standard key derivation function, with a label saying which key is wanted. The result is the same on both sides, and the shared secret never travels over the network.

sections.title: Which Parts of a Message Are Protected
sections.content:
OSCORE transforms a CoAP message into an OSCORE message and vice versa, protecting as much of the original message as possible while still allowing certain proxy operations. Message fields of the CoAP message may be protected end to end in three ways: Class E, encrypted and integrity protected; Class I, integrity protected only; and Class U, unprotected.

The sending endpoint SHALL transfer Class E message fields in the ciphertext of the COSE object. It SHALL include Class I message fields in the additional authenticated data of the AEAD algorithm, allowing the receiving endpoint to detect if the value has changed in transfer. Class U message fields SHALL NOT be protected in transfer, and Class I and Class U values are transferred in the header or options part of the OSCORE message, which is visible to proxies.

Message fields not visible to proxies, transported in the ciphertext, are called Inner. Message fields transferred in the header or options part, visible to proxies, are called Outer. There are currently no Class I options defined. An OSCORE message may contain both an Inner and an Outer instance of a certain CoAP message field: Inner fields are intended for the receiving endpoint, while Outer fields are used to enable proxy operations.

Options that are unknown, or for which OSCORE processing is not defined, SHALL be processed as Class E. Specifications of new CoAP options SHOULD define how they are processed with OSCORE, and a new option SHOULD be of Class E unless it requires proxy processing. The table of options in the RFC shows, for example, that Uri-Host, Uri-Port, Proxy-Uri and Proxy-Scheme are Class U because a proxy needs them, while Uri-Path and Uri-Query are Class E.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of a message is put in one of three buckets: hidden and encrypted, visible but tamper-proof, or simply visible. A forwarder only needs the third kind, such as the host name and the port, so everything else can stay secret.

sections.title: The Protected Object and the Nonce
sections.content:
The protected data is carried in an untagged COSE_Encrypt0 structure using an AEAD algorithm. The protected field is empty. The unprotected field includes the Partial IV parameter, whose value is the Sender Sequence Number with leading zero bytes removed, and the kid parameter, whose value is the Sender ID. Both are normally present in requests and not in responses. A kid context parameter, carrying the ID Context, may be present in requests. The ciphertext field is computed from the secret key, the AEAD nonce, the plaintext and the additional authenticated data.

The plaintext is a CoAP message with a subset of the header: the Code of the original message, all Inner option message fields present in the original message, and the payload if present, prefixed by the one-byte payload marker 0xff.

The additional authenticated data is a CBOR array wrapped in a byte string, holding the OSCORE version number, which implementations MUST set to 1, an array of algorithms, the kid of the request, the Partial IV of the request, and the Class I options of the original message. The version and algorithm values are agreed out of band, and the additional data lets both ends check that they agree. The AAD is the array ["Encrypt0", h'', external_aad]; in the example given it consists of a fixed string of 11 bytes concatenated with the external additional data.

The nonce is built in four steps: left-pad the Partial IV with zeroes to exactly 5 bytes, left-pad the Sender ID of the endpoint that generated the Partial IV with zeroes to exactly the nonce length minus 6 bytes, concatenate the size of that ID as a single byte with the padded ID and the padded Partial IV, and then XOR the result with the Common IV. Only AEAD algorithms that use nonces of at least 7 bytes are supported. If the Partial IV is not present in a response, the nonce from the request is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The encrypted blob contains the code of the request, the protected options and the payload. A number that counts requests goes into the message and is mixed into the nonce, so that the same key is never used with the same nonce twice.

sections.title: Making the Messages Small
sections.content:
CBOR combines very small message sizes with extensibility, and COSE uses it to create compact encodings of signed and encrypted data. However, COSE is constructed to support a large number of different stateless use cases and is not fully optimized for use as a stateful security protocol, leading to a larger than necessary message expansion. OSCORE therefore defines a stateless header compression mechanism, simply removing redundant information from the COSE objects, which significantly reduces the per-packet overhead. The result is called the compressed COSE object.

The value of the OSCORE option contains the flag bits, the Partial IV, the kid context and the kid. The first byte holds the flags: the three least significant bits encode the Partial IV length n, where n equal to 0 means the Partial IV is not present and the values 6 and 7 are reserved; the fourth bit is the kid flag, set to 1 if the kid is present; the fifth bit is the kid context flag, set to 1 if a kid context is present; and the sixth to eighth bits are reserved for future use and SHALL be set to zero when not in use, with a message being considered malformed if any of them is set to 1. The following n bytes encode the Partial IV, the following byte encodes the length s of the kid context if the kid context flag is set, the following s bytes encode the kid context, and the remaining bytes encode the kid. The kid MUST be the last field of the option value.

The payload of the OSCORE message SHALL encode the ciphertext of the COSE object. The RFC's examples show a request whose compressed object is 17 bytes against 24 bytes before compression: a flag byte of 0x09, an option value of 0x090525 and a 14-byte payload.
sections.plainLanguage: Standard encrypted-message formats carry a lot of repeated information. OSCORE strips that repetition out, so the protection adds as little to the message as possible, which matters when the device has to send over a slow link.

sections.title: Binding, Freshness and Replay
sections.content:
OSCORE binds responses to the requests by including the kid and Partial IV of the request in the additional authenticated data of the response, which prevents response delay and mismatch attacks by on-path attackers and compromised intermediaries. The server therefore needs to store the kid and Partial IV of the request until all responses have been sent. Both endpoints MUST keep the association of the token, the security context and the Partial IV of the request, so that the right context can be found and the right additional data computed for the response.

An AEAD nonce MUST NOT be used more than once per AEAD key, and if messages are processed concurrently, reading and increasing the Sender Sequence Number MUST be atomic. The maximum Sender Sequence Number is algorithm dependent and SHALL be less than 2^40; if the number exceeds the maximum, the endpoint MUST NOT process any more messages with that Sender Context and SHOULD acquire a new security context. The RFC's security considerations give the maximum as 2^40 - 1.

For requests, OSCORE provides only the guarantee that the request is not older than the security context; applications with stronger demands, such as control of actuators, need extra freshness mechanisms. Assuming an honest server, the message binding guarantees that a response is not older than its request, which gives absolute freshness for a single response, while for notifications the guarantee weakens over time and it is RECOMMENDED that the client regularly re-register the observation.

To protect against replay of requests, the server's Recipient Context includes a Replay Window. The server SHALL verify that the Sender Sequence Number received in the Partial IV has not been received before, and if the verification fails it SHALL stop processing the message and MAY respond with a 4.01 Unauthorized error. Over a reliable and ordered transport the server MAY store only the last received Partial IV and require that newly received ones equal it plus 1, while over mixed transports the default window may be more suitable. The operation of validating the Partial IV and updating the replay protection MUST be atomic.

Endpoints must also handle losing the rapidly changing parts of the context, such as the Sender Sequence Number and the Replay Window, which are typically stored in RAM and lost on a reboot. The alternatives are to reuse the context after updating its mutable parts, to derive new contexts from the same shared Master Secret, or to use a trusted third-party-assisted key establishment protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Each request carries a counter, and the server remembers which counters it has seen so that a recorded message cannot be replayed. The reply is tied to the request that caused it, so a reply cannot be swapped for another one later.
